stories.title: Consumer Goods Companies Scrutinize CRE Portfolios As Technology Spending Lags
stories.excerpt: Consumer goods companies are focusing on supply chain disruptions and shifts in consumer spending habits to better manage their real estate portfolios, according to a JLL report. The company’s findings are based on 48 responses from consumer goods industry leaders. Close to 48% of respondents said their organizations The firm’s latest corporate real estate pulse survey included 48 responses from consumer goods industry leaders. Nearly 48% of respondents said their organizations are examining supply chains, “a notable 10 percentage points above the all-industry rate of 37.9% and the sharpest gap among priorities tracked in the survey,” according to JLL. While the data is essential for decision-making, JLL said that technology investment has yet to catch up, with 16.7% of consumer goods respondents anticipating growth in their CRE technology budgets over the next three years, compared to 30.6% across all industries. Also being examined is the workforce, as 39.6% of respondents said they’ve downsized their labor, compared to 31.6% across industries. Additionally, 37.5% said they expect office use rates to increase over the next 12 months. At the same time, 31.3% of respondents expect their CRE budgets to increase, compared to 24% across industries. “Where those dollars go matters: upgrades for higher production, space for more employees, or better utilization data that reveals opportunities to consolidate or redirect investment,” according to JLL. JLL recommended building a reliable data foundation, using technology to increase capacity and implementing a flexible portfolio strategy. “A shopper can put one product back on the shelf,” the report said. “A consumer goods company has to decide what happens to the factory, warehouse, office or brand behind it. That decision starts with knowing what you have.” The post Consumer Goods Companies Scrutinize CRE Portfolios As Technology Spending Lags appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: 48% of consumer goods firms examining supply chains vs. 37.9% all industries
39.6% downsized labor; 37.5% expect office use rates to increase next 12 months
Only 16.7% anticipate CRE tech budget growth vs. 30.6% across all industries
stories.summary: Consumer goods companies are prioritizing supply chain optimization and labor restructuring ahead of technology investment. Nearly 40% have downsized workforces, yet 37.5% expect office utilization to rise. Despite heightened CRE portfolio scrutiny, only 16.7% plan to increase tech budgets over three years, well below the all-industry average of 30.6%.
stories.impact: Reduced consumer goods labor forces and delayed tech spending signal weaker near-term office absorption and potential real estate rationalization in supply-chain hubs (e.g., Chicago, Houston, LA ports). This signals headwinds for speculative office conversion; multifamily in logistics-adjacent submarkets may face softer ancillary job demand despite supply chain focus.

stories.title: Healthcare Real Estate Utilization: More Than Vacancy Data
stories.excerpt: Healthcare systems spend a great deal of time and effort toward improving patient access, operating margins, physician productivity and capital allocation. But real estate portfolio performance is most often analyzed through occupancy, which isn’t enough. In its recent report, “Beyond Vacancy: A Maturity Model for Measuring Healthcare Space Utilization,” Newmark suggested that healthcare organizations should dig deeper into measuring real estate performance. Facilities, strategy and real estate teams together “possess the information needed to transform real estate from an operational necessity into a strategic asset,” the report said. The problem is that these groups aren’t integrated, which means decision-making information tends to be disconnected and ineffective. Newmark proposed a five-level maturity model to provide a framework for integrating perspectives. Level 1: Occupancy status. The first step is to determine whether the clinical space is occupied or empty. Combining the information with square footage and occupancy costs can help identify properties that consume resources without actively supporting patient care. Data source: facilities. Level 2: Square feet per exam room. Comparing facilities against internal design standards or relevant benchmarks helps measure physical design efficiency. A careful analysis can uncover inefficient layouts, oversized support areas and excess circulation space. Data source: facilities and design standards Level 3: Static provider occupancy. Adding provider assignments to the mix provides a clearer picture of operational capacity, assuming the healthcare staff uses the space full-time. A clinic that is assigned six providers differs from one assigned two providers, even if both have the same amount of space. Data source: provider assignments. Level 4: Dynamic provider occupancy. bullets: Healthcare organizations lack integrated real estate and operations decision-making
Newmark proposes five-level maturity model to measure space utilization beyond occupancy
Lease renewals often commit before operational needs are understood
stories.summary: Healthcare real estate decisions are fragmented across facilities, strategy, and clinical teams, resulting in poor capital allocation. Newmark's maturity model framework emphasizes measuring how real estate supports care delivery rather than maximizing activity per square foot. The issue is structural: healthcare lease commitments require long-term decisions before operational needs are fully known.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily impact; healthcare asset strategy misalignment affects office/MOB portfolios, not apartment demand. However, if healthcare systems rationalize real estate footprints in secondary markets (rural hospitals consolidating), workforce migration out of those submarkets could reduce multifamily demand fundamentals.

stories.title: CBRE: Hybrid Work Can Mean Hidden Risks for Office Incentives
stories.excerpt: Hybrid work might be a good strategy for some companies. It keeps employees happy, which can lead to better retention rates. However, a recent CBRE report said that the rapid adoption of the hybrid work model also means new compliance risks for companies receiving local and state economic incentives. Companies face a fragmented landscape where temporary pandemic allowances have expired, state rules conflict with local mandates, and compliance definitions often compromise current benefit collections,” the report said. Part of the reason is that organizations today are relying on economic development incentives written and enacted before 2020. State and local authorities have enacted requirements for hybrid work models. However, “on-site physical attendance requirements now range from 0% to nearly 60% of a standard work week,” CBRE said. At the same time, companies that don’t meet jurisdictional requirements could lose benefits, face financial penalties or risk violating multi-year employment commitments. Three common incentive compliance risks include the following: Expiration of temporary allowances. Pandemic-era relief in many jurisdictions has expired without formal notice. Companies that rely on those allowances after they have expired could be considered retroactively non-compliant. Misapplication to retained employees. Compliance rules can apply to new hires and retained positions. Existing remote workers can’t be grandfathered into meeting the new attendance requirements. Credit reductions and contract defaults. A reduction of on-site employees reduces the credits a company can claim, resulting in clawbacks or other penalties related to multi-year retention commitments. The implications of compliance risk are huge for organizations. It should also be considered when seeking a suitable site for these companies. “Companies engaging in site selection need to consider their workforce mix at the start of the project,” CBRE said. bullets: State on-site attendance mandates range from 0% to 60% of work week
Companies risk losing economic development incentives if hybrid policies violate compliance
Incentive rules written pre-2020 conflict with current hybrid work allowances
stories.summary: CBRE warns that rapid hybrid work adoption creates compliance risks for companies receiving state and local economic development incentives. Jurisdictions have imposed varying on-site attendance thresholds (0–60%) and allowed pandemic-era flexibility to expire, creating legal and financial exposure. Companies failing to meet requirements face penalty, forfeiture of benefits, and multi-year employment commitment violations.
stories.impact: In markets with aggressive incentive clawback risk (Texas, Florida, Sun Belt tech hubs), employers may lock office occupancy higher than they otherwise prefer to protect abatements and PILOT programs. This artificially props up demand for office space and subdues hybrid-enabled workforce flexibility, reducing net migration of remote workers into secondary markets and flattening multifamily demand pressure in otherwise high-growth submarkets.

stories.title: Slower Job Growth Shifts CRE Demand and Investment Strategies
stories.excerpt: The U.S. economy may need to add fewer than 50,000 jobs per month to keep unemployment stable, according to a recent Marcus & Millichap report. The number represents a shift from the 100,000 monthly jobs that were previously required. The reason? Marcus & Millichap said that demographic changes, rising worker productivity and reduced immigration are affecting labor market dynamics, which, in turn, will affect commercial real estate demand and investment. What the Job Numbers Say The economy added just 29,000 jobs in September, while downward revisions to July and August erased another 60,000 jobs from previously reported gains. Year-to-date job gains stand at 612,000, and Moody’s forecasts gains of 735,000 for full-year 2026 and 645,000 in 2027. Despite weaker hiring, unemployment has remained in the low-4% range. Retirements and reduced net immigration are constraining labor force growth. According to economist Gad Levanon, real productivity in professional and business services was up 16% from its 2019 level. Marcus & Millichap said that these trends, as a whole, support a stable employment rate with fewer new jobs needed. What it Means for CRE The impact of these numbers on commercial real estate is uneven. For multifamily, weaker employment growth means a reduction in household formation, a decrease in absorption and downward pressure on work-related migration. This is especially true in the Sun Belt markets, which continue to grapple with excess supply amid moderating demand. Meanwhile, retail continues robust, thanks to consumer spending. Consumer sales increased 6% year over year through August, or about 2.5% after adjusting for inflation. On the flip side, those numbers haven’t led to more demand for retail space. Net absorption has averaged less than 2 million square feet per quarter since the beginning of 2025, down from more than 6 million square feet per quarter in 2024 and 12 million square feet per quarter in 2019. bullets: U.S. needs only ~50K jobs/month to sustain low unemployment, down from 100K
September added 29K jobs; YTD 612K; Moody's forecasts 735K for full-year 2026
Productivity up 16% since 2019; retirements and reduced immigration constraining labor growth
stories.summary: Job growth requirements have halved to under 50,000 monthly due to demographic headwinds, productivity gains, and immigration constraints. September's weak 29,000 payroll gain and 60,000 downward revisions signal a labor market losing momentum despite low unemployment. Moody's forecasts only 735,000 net jobs for full-year 2026, implying flat-to-negative net migration and softer population inflows.
stories.impact: Materially weaker national job growth and labor force expansion directly compress multifamily demand fundamentals—fewer inbound workers and reduced household formation. Secondary and Sunbelt markets that depended on migration-driven growth will see rent growth decelerate; development windows are narrowing. Underwriting assumptions for renter household growth, in-migration, and occupancy will need downward revision across most markets through 2027.

stories.title: Prologis Expects More Development, Acquisitions as Industrial Recovery Grows
stories.excerpt: Prologis executives told investors Thursday the company anticipates putting more shovels in the ground and buying more property after the third quarter of 2026, but also warned that higher interest rates could slow transaction activity. The world’s largest warehouse landlord signed 60 million square feet of leases during the third quarter, CEO Dan Letter said on the company’s earnings call. Average occupancy improved to 95.1 percent, compared to 94.8 percent a year earlier. The San Francisco-based real estate investment trust (REIT) generated $2.39 billion in third-quarter revenue, down slightly from $2.43 billion in the second quarter, but up from $2.21 billion a year ago. Core funds from operations totaled $1.55 billion, or $1.60 per diluted share. That compares with $1.56 billion in the second quarter, and $1.43 billion in the third quarter last year. Chief Financial Officer Tim Arndt said the company acquired about $702 million of real estate in the third quarter, compared to $1.12 billion in the second quarter and just $48 million in third-quarter 2025. Net income attributable to common shareholders came to $816 million, down from $1.06 billion in the second quarter, but above the $763 million reported during the same quarter last year. Prologis also stepped up its outlook for capital deployment. The company increased its 2026 acquisition guidance to between $2.1 billion and $2.3 billion, up from $1.5 billion to $2 billion. The REIT anticipates an especially active finish to the year on the construction side, too. Prologis now expects to finish the year with between $5 billion and $5.75 billion in new development, up from its previous expectation of $4.5 billion to $5.5 billion. During the quarter, Prologis started about $1 billion worth of development, bringing year-to-date starts to nearly $5 billion. bullets: Prologis signed 60M SF leases Q3; occupancy improved to 95.1% from 94.8% YoY
Acquired $702M real estate Q3 vs. $48M Q3 2025; anticipates more development post-Q3 2026
Higher interest rates could slow transaction activity; Q3 revenue $2.39B, core FFO $1.60/share
stories.summary: Prologis, the world's largest industrial REIT, showed strong Q3 leasing momentum (60M SF) and occupancy gains, signaling robust demand. The company deployed $702M in acquisitions and plans to accelerate development and M&A after Q3 2026. However, management flagged elevated interest rates as a potential brake on transaction velocity going forward.
stories.impact: Industrial fundamentals remain robust, but Prologis's caution on rate sensitivity suggests cap rates may not compress further and development feasibility windows are tightening. For multifamily developers, this signals competitive pressure for construction labor and materials in logistics-adjacent markets; industrial's strength continues to bid up hard costs. In markets with concurrent multifamily and industrial construction (Dallas, Phoenix, Atlanta), cost inflation and labor scarcity will persist.

stories.title: JLL Arranges Krispy Kreme Leases as Brand Grows Tri-State Presence
stories.excerpt: JLL has secured three retail leases totaling 3,250 square feet on behalf of Krispy Kreme across New Jersey and New York, part of the doughnut brand’s continued expansion throughout the New York metropolitan area. The leases include locations in Marlboro and Ocean Township, NJ and in Brooklyn.Managing director David Townes, based in JLL’s Parsippany, NJ office, represented Krispy Kreme in all three transactions, securing locations across established suburban shopping destinations and dense urban retail corridors. “These three transactions reflect Krispy Kreme’s strategic approach to expanding its presence across the New York metropolitan area,” said Townes. “As the brand continues its regional expansion, identifying well-positioned retail spaces that align with its operational needs and customer base will remain a key priority.” The transactions come as Krispy Kreme announces a new franchise development agreement with longtime franchise partner Original Entrepreneurs LLC to open 33 additional shops across the region over the next five years. The post JLL Arranges Krispy Kreme Leases as Brand Grows Tri-State Presence appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Krispy Kreme leasing 3,250 SF across Marlboro NJ, Ocean Township NJ, and Brooklyn
Franchise partner Original Entrepreneurs to open 33 additional shops over five years
Expansion targets established suburban shopping destinations and dense urban corridors
stories.summary: Krispy Kreme is expanding aggressively across the New York metropolitan area through direct leases and a franchise development agreement for 33 units over five years. The brand is targeting both suburban shopping centers and urban retail corridors in New Jersey and New York, signaling confidence in tri-state consumer demand.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily relevance; retail expansion signals underlying population and consumer confidence in NYC tri-state but does not imply new job creation or inbound migration beyond existing trends. Retail leasing activity in NY/NJ can indicate retail market health and ground-floor economics in mixed-use development, but does not alter multifamily supply or demand forecasts materially.

stories.title: Cushman & Wakefield Hires CBRE’s Doug Middleton as Head of Capital Markets
stories.excerpt: Doug Middleton and Jack Stillwagon have left CBRE for one of its global competitors. Middleton has joined Cushman & Wakefield to lead its institutional capital markets business in New York City while Stillwagon will serve as executive managing director. Both Middleton and Stillwagon start in their new roles today. An industry veteran, Middleton previously spent eight years at CBRE, most recently leading its Investment Properties Institutional Group, with Stillwagon working alongside him and focusing primarily on office, residential and industrial transactions. Now, the two will bring their combined experience to the table at 1290 Avenue of the Americas, collaborating with the brokerage’s teams nationally to further its business and capital markets reach. “New York is essential to Cushman & Wakefield’s institutional capital markets strategy,” Miles Treaster, president of Americas Capital Markets, said in a statement. “Doug and Jack bring deep transaction experience and client relationships to the firm. Their partnership will strengthen our New York capital markets presence and more effectively connect our regional clients with our national and global platform.” Middleton has executed billions of dollars of transactions over the years, including the sale of 450 Park Avenue to SL Green in April 2022 for $455 million and Sotheby’s $410 million sale of 1334 York Avenue to Weill Cornell Medicine in 2025. Prior to CBRE, Middleton was a director of investment sales at Eastdil Secured. Stillwagon joined CBRE in 2021, and previously held positions at Waterfall Properties and Atlantic Creek Real Estate Partners. Jack Stillwagon. PHOTO: Courtesy CBRE Middleton described his big move as an “exciting opportunity.” “The leadership here has cultivated an exceptional culture in New York City, providing my team and me with the support and empowerment needed to deliver top-tier results for our clients,” he said in a statement. “I’m eager to enter this next chapter of my career
bullets: Doug Middleton and Jack Stillwagon exit CBRE for Cushman & Wakefield
Middleton leads institutional capital markets; duo brings 8+ years CBRE office, residential, industrial experience
Hire reinforces C&W's New York capital markets push and national institutional client network
stories.summary: Cushman & Wakefield hired two senior CBRE capital markets veterans, Middleton and Stillwagon, to expand its New York institutional investment business. Middleton previously led CBRE's Investment Properties Institutional Group, focusing on office, residential, and industrial transactions. The move bolsters C&W's national capital markets platform and NYC presence.
stories.impact: Broker talent migration does not change market fundamentals but can signal a shift in capital markets positioning or client relationships. No direct impact on multifamily supply, demand, or cost; lateral hire announcements are noise unless accompanied by portfolio mandates or capital redeployment signals.

stories.title: Colorado Federal Bank Lends $23M for Brooklyn Apartments at Former Event Space
stories.excerpt: Double U Development has sealed $23 million of construction financing to transform a former Brooklyn music and wedding venue into apartments, Commercial Observer has learned. Colorado Federal Bank supplied the loan for the developer’s 60-unit multifamily project at 144 Greenpoint Avenue in Brooklyn’s Greenpoint neighborhood. The site was home to the Polonaise Terrace wedding venue until 2016 before turning into the Brooklyn Bazaar concert hall. Double U acquired the property for $8.9 million in January 2026 from MacArthur Holdings nearly seven years after Brooklyn Bazaar was closed. Parallel CRE’s Richard Sutton negotiated the debt, which also retires past land acquisition debt in addition to funding construction costs. Michael Weitzman, founder and CEO of Double U, filed plans in May 2025 to turn the vacant two-story property into a multifamily and retail building, CO reported at the time. Double U is planning an eight-story building slated for completion in 2028. Total project costs are estimated at $30 million with the $23 million loan funding 100 percent of the go-forward construction costs, according to Sutton. The development received necessary approvals from New York City’s Landmarks Preservation Commission and qualified for a 485-x tax exemption since a portion of the units will be designated as affordable housing. Colorado Federal Bank and Double U Development did not immediately return requests for comment. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Colorado Federal Bank provided $23M construction loan for Double U's 60-unit project
144 Greenpoint Ave, Brooklyn; conversion of former Polonaise Terrace and Brooklyn Bazaar venues
Total project cost $30M; eight-story building targeted for completion in 2028
stories.summary: Double U Development secured $23M in construction financing from Colorado Federal Bank to convert a vacant Brooklyn event venue into a 60-unit apartment building at 144 Greenpoint Avenue in Greenpoint. The $30M project includes retail and is slated to deliver in 2028. The loan also retired prior acquisition debt dating to the January 2026 land purchase.
stories.impact: Direct supply signal: 60 units of new multifamily housing delivering to Brooklyn Greenpoint in 2028, a tight supply market. Lender willingness to finance adaptive reuse at this scale and leverage indicates continued debt availability for residential development despite higher rates. Project timeline (2 years out) suggests developer confidence in Brooklyn market fundamentals and absorption.

stories.title: EQT Real Estate Acquires $16B Alternatives Investment Firm Stockbridge for $375M
stories.excerpt: EQT Real Estate, the commercial real estate subsidiary of Swedish private equity giant EQT AB, announced Thursday that it has acquired Stockbridge, a U.S. real estate investment firm with $16.5 billion in assets, for $375 million. The deal, which includes an option to pay out $175 million in performance-based bonuses over the next four years, delivers industrial assets and alternatives such as industrial outdoor storage and manufactured housing into EQT’s portfolio, but largely keeps in place the Stockbridge leadership and investment teams. The deal also ensures Stockbridge’s real estate funds strategies — primarily its open-ended core products — will operate independently within EQT Real Estate’s broader investment network. Under the terms of the agreement, EQT Real Estate takes 100 percent control of Stockbridge and any general partner entities within the firm’s numerous real estate investment funds, and will invest 35 percent of any carried interest into future funds established by Stockbridge. Per Franzén, CEO and managing partner of EQT AB, called the deal “a significant next step in the development” of the firm’s real estate investment business and said the newly combined entity will broaden approaches into new sectors thanks to Stockbridge’s diversified portfolio in the U.S. alternatives space. “Stockbridge has built an impressive track record over more than two decades and is an excellent fit with EQT Real Estate,” said Franzén. “Both sides will learn and develop from one another while contributing to the wider EQT platform.” Stockbridge was founded in 2002, and today employs 185 professionals across six U.S. offices. EQT Real Estate was established only in 2021, following EQT AB’s $1.9 billion acquisition of Exeter Property Group, but has doubled in size within the last five years. bullets: EQT Real Estate acquired Stockbridge for $375M plus $175M performance earn-out
Stockbridge manages $16.5B in AUM; adds industrial assets and manufactured housing
EQT takes 100% control; Stockbridge leadership retained; 35% of carried interest reinvested
stories.summary: Swedish PE giant EQT AB's real estate subsidiary acquired Stockbridge, a $16.5B alternative real estate fund manager, for $375M upfront plus up to $175M in performance bonuses. The deal expands EQT's industrial and alternatives platform, including manufactured housing, while preserving Stockbridge's fund strategies and leadership. EQT commits to reinvesting 35% of carried interest into future Stockbridge funds.
stories.impact: Significant capital inflow into alternatives and industrial real estate; Stockbridge's manufactured housing focus signals institutional PE confidence in that subsector. For multifamily developers, this reinforces industrial/logistics investor appetite but signals competing capital pools for alternative housing strategies (MH, co-living, etc.). No direct supply or demand effect, but indicates deepening alternative-asset institutionalization that may siphon capital from core multifamily development.

stories.title: Sustainability Innovation Equals Improved Building Performance: Forum
stories.excerpt: Watch the full video recap here. Commercial real estate executives have made the case for the practicality of implementing sustainability in their portfolios beyond just societal expectations. Commercial Observer on Wednesday hosted its virtual Sustainability Forum: The Cutting-Edge Innovations Transforming Business, in which panelists discussed the reasons why they view sustainability as a good financial decision and how they are scaling innovation to not only meet tenant demand, but also to save money down the line. Emceed by Cathy Cunningham, CO’s executive editor, the event started off with a panel called From Policy to Portfolio Performance: How ESG Regulation is Reshaping Institutional Real Estate Investment, moderated by Evolution Sustainability Group’s Chuck Hurchalla. Others on the panel were Empire State Realty Trust’s Dana Schneider, Silverstein Properties’ Jonathan Hong, Kilroy Realty’s Sarah King and Greystar’s Cope Willis. (ESG is short for environmental, social and corporate governance.) The takeaway? Policies are inconsistent across different markets, so it’s best to be forward-thinking and invest in the latest technology, which also tends to be the most sustainable. Commercial Observer’s Sustainability Forum panel: Ben Myers, Apaulo Malloy, Elizabeth Redmond, Lisa Brylowski, Scott Thomsen. SCREENSHOT: Commercial Observer “It makes sense to invest in these things whether it’s for compliance or not,” Schneider said. “Most major cities in the U.S. and many abroad have policies that can be inconsistent, even between the U.K. and the E.U., and there are a lot of inconsistencies in America. There is no federal policy here. … In absence of regulation, what we have focused on is to look at the life cycle of our assets and major equipment, and do long-term planning.” The second, and last, panel of the day, The Real Value of Sustainability: The Importance of ESG in Sourcing Capital & Driving Asset Valuations, was moderated by R-Zero’s Elizabeth Redm
bullets: CRE executives view sustainability as financial decision, not just ESG compliance
Panelists include Empire State Realty Trust, Silverstein, Kilroy Realty, Greystar leadership
Sustainability drives tenant demand, operational savings, and portfolio performance improvements
stories.summary: Commercial Observer's Sustainability Forum featured institutional real estate leaders making the case for sustainability as financial strategy. Panelists from Empire State Realty Trust, Silverstein Properties, Kilroy Realty, and Greystar discussed how ESG measures improve tenant retention, reduce operating costs, and enhance long-term asset value beyond regulatory compliance.
stories.impact: Sustainability and ESG are increasingly priced into institutional cap rate expectations and tenant demand (especially for larger operators). Multifamily developers must budget for green building standards (LEED, Net Zero, electric-ready) as tenant preference and lender/investor requirement, raising development costs 5–15%. Markets with strong ESG renter demand (tech hubs, urban centers) will favor sustainable new supply; projects without green credentials face leasing and refinance headwinds.
